contents: [Chief Complaint]: Patient Jiang Luoyu, 69 years old, was admitted to the hospital on October 19, 2007, due to a six-month history of distension and pain in the lower abdomen and lumbosacral region. [Present History]: The patient is a 22-year postmenopausal elderly woman, with her first pregnancy at age 19, G8P7, and an intrauterine device (IUD) placed for 34 years. Six months ago, she developed distension and pain in the lower abdomen and lumbosacral region, which recurred, accompanied by urinary frequency and urgency, without dysuria; she often had constipation. She had no **vaginal bleeding or discharge, no external genital pruritus, etc. She assumed it was due to IUD displacement and did not seek timely treatment. Later, due to the worsening of the aforementioned symptoms, she had the IUD removed at an outside hospital. Preoperative ultrasound examination revealed a solid mass in the uterus (considered uterine fibroid), leading her to seek treatment at our hospital. During the course of the illness, her mental status, sleep, and appetite were good, and there was no weight loss. [Past History]: None. [Physical Examination]: T 36.7°C, P 74 beats/min, BP 130/80 mmHg, normal development, average nutrition, clear consciousness, clear speech, cooperative with examination, slender build; no abnormalities in heart and lungs; slightly distended abdomen, no tenderness, liver and spleen not palpable, a mass palpable in the pelvis, upper boundary between the umbilicus and pubis, clear margins, hard, fixed, no obvious tenderness, no shifting dullness in the abdomen; gynecological examination: atrophic vulva and **, no abnormal findings, right fornix obliterated, lower boundary of the pelvic mass palpable, atrophic cervix, no abnormal appearance; uterus enlarged to the size of a 4-month pregnancy, hard, immobile, clear margins, mild tenderness; bilateral adnexa not clearly palpable. [Auxiliary Examinations]: Blood analysis showed no abnormalities, liver and kidney function normal, chest X-ray showed no abnormalities in both lungs, no abnormalities in urinalysis. [Auxiliary Examinations]: Ultrasound showed: uterus size 14.0×12.8×10.0 CM3, mid-position, full contour, heterogeneous实质回声, multiple hypoechoic masses seen in the uterine body, unclear borders, ultrasound diagnosis: multiple solid masses in the uterus (considered adenomyosis with fibroids). Please infer the patient's possible preliminary diagnosis based on the above medical information?

[Chief Complaint]: Zhi ××, male, adult.
He ××, female, 46 years old. [Current Medical History]: Dyspepsia and heartburn for more than one year. Diagnosed with chronic gastritis by a physician. Initially, acid-suppressing agents were effective, but symptoms recurred immediately upon discontinuation. Subsequently, a Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) practitioner prescribed cuttlebone, cicada slough, and Zhejiang贝 (Zhejiang贝 should be Zhejiang贝母, which is Zhejiang Fritillary Bulb in English) and other herbs, which provided temporary relief, but symptoms recurred upon discontinuation. Later, another physician diagnosed it as cold in the stomach, and after one dose, the burning sensation decreased, but further doses caused oral ulcers. Subsequently, it was diagnosed as heat in the stomach, and although the oral ulcers improved, the burning sensation and dyspepsia worsened. Upon detailed examination, in addition to dyspepsia and heartburn, the patient also experienced a bitter and dry mouth, thin white tongue coating, and wiry and涩 (stringy and涩 should be stringy and rough) pulse. After comprehensive evaluation of the pulse and symptoms, it was concluded that this was a case of mixed cold and heat, with more cold than heat. A formula with a bitter and pungent nature to descend and harmonize, with more heat than cold, was prescribed.
For one year, dyspepsia and heartburn, bitter and dry mouth. Diagnosed with chronic gastritis. Initially treated with Western medicine, symptoms slightly improved, but recurred upon discontinuation. Subsequently treated with TCM herbs such as cuttlebone and瓦楞子 (瓦楞子 should be Calamariae Concha, which is Limestone Shell in English), with similar results to Western medicine. Later, various TCM practitioners were consulted, with some diagnosing it as cold and others as heat, but all treatments were ineffective. Upon detailed examination, in addition to heartburn, the patient also experienced dry mouth and slippery pulse. Therefore, the patient was prescribed Ban Xia Xie Xin Tang. Prescription: Pinellia ternata 10 grams, Coptis chinensis 10 grams, Scutellaria baicalensis 10 grams, dried ginger 10 grams, Codonopsis pilosula 10 grams, glycyrrhiza 6 grams, jujube 7 pieces. After 4 doses, symptoms significantly improved, and after 20 doses, the patient recovered. [Past Medical History]: None. [Physical Examination]: None. [Auxiliary Examinations]: None. Please infer the possible preliminary diagnosis based on the above medical information?

[Chief Complaint]: Right upper quadrant colic pain with nausea and vomiting for 6 hours, came to the clinic at 3:40 AM today. [Present Illness]: The patient has experienced abdominal distension and right upper quadrant pain, described as colicky, after consuming greasy food and physical exertion (drying rice) over the past few days, which started around 10 PM last night. The pain is intermittent and radiates to the right chest, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and two episodes of vomiting of gastric contents, chills, and no fever. There is no pain in the left upper quadrant or lower abdomen, and no referred pain to the left shoulder. The patient had three bowel movements last night, which were formed but in small amounts each time. Appetite and urination are normal, but the patient is restless and has been **. In June this year, the patient had a similar episode and was diagnosed with acute cholecystitis at a health center, treated with intravenous fluids for one week until recovery. The specific medications used are unknown, and no ultrasound or blood routine examination was performed at that time. [Past Medical History]: The patient had pulmonary tuberculosis 10 years ago, and underwent an appendectomy due to acute appendicitis perforation 5 years ago. One and a half years after the appendectomy, the surgical scar split due to carrying rice, necessitating another surgery. The patient has a history of chronic gastritis but denies a history of hepatitis, diabetes, hypertension, or heart disease. Personal History: G3P3 menstrual type: age 18, 3-4 days/30-40 days, dysmenorrhea. Tubal ligation was performed at the age of 23. [Physical Examination]: Temperature 36°C, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, heart rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 160/100 mmHg. The patient is alert but in poor spirits, with a painful appearance and has been **. The patient is obese and has been holding the right upper quadrant while walking to the clinic. There is no icterus of the skin or sclera, and no enlarged superficial lymph nodes. The throat is normal, and the heart and lungs are normal. The abdomen is soft with no visible intestinal pattern or peristaltic waves. A surgical scar of about 10 cm is visible in the right lower abdomen, and a surgical scar of about 3 cm is visible in the midline of the lower abdomen. The right upper quadrant shows muscle tension, tenderness, and rebound tenderness. Murphy's sign is positive. Due to the patient's obesity, an enlarged gallbladder is not palpable. Bowel sounds are hyperactive on auscultation. There is no tenderness on percussion over the renal areas, no edema in the lower extremities, and normal limb movement. Physiological reflexes are present, and no other pathological reflexes are elicited. [Auxiliary Examinations]: (None yet) Please infer the possible preliminary diagnosis based on the above medical information?

[Chief Complaint]: Female patient, 29 years old, married, civil servant.
Admitted due to abdominal pain and vomiting for two days. [Current Medical History]: Two days ago, the patient developed upper abdominal pain without any obvious cause, which was intermittent, accompanied by nausea and frequent vomiting, with vomitus being gastric contents, and associated with abdominal distension and pain. The patient had one episode of yellow loose stool with no abnormal volume, and has not passed gas or stool for the past day. The local hospital treated her for "acute gastritis" with "anti-infection, antispasmodic, and fluid replacement" therapies, but the symptoms did not improve. The abdominal pain became persistently worse, accompanied by fever with a temperature reaching 38.0°C, but without hematemesis, hematochezia, or oliguria. She was transferred to our hospital for further diagnosis and treatment. Outpatient examination of blood routine and abdominal X-ray resulted in admission with a diagnosis of "intestinal obstruction." Past Medical History: The patient has no history of peptic ulcer disease or similar abdominal pain. She underwent a cesarean section surgery at a local hospital 4 years ago. [Past Medical History]: None. [Physical Examination]: T: 37.8°C, P: 112 beats/min, R: 22 breaths/min, BP: 90/60 mmHg.
Acute illness appearance, indifferent expression, delayed response, lethargic, cachectic, and dehydrated. No petechiae or rash on the skin, superficial lymph nodes not enlarged. Bilateral sunken eyeballs, no icterus of the sclera, no cyanosis of the lips, dry and red tongue. Soft neck, trachea midline. Reduced skin turgor over the sternum, clear breath sounds in both lungs, no dry or wet rales heard. Cardiac borders not enlarged, heart rate 112 beats/min, regular rhythm, strong heart sounds, no murmurs heard in all valve areas. Abdomen distended and symmetrical, no visible gastric or intestinal patterns or peristaltic waves, negative for Cullen's sign and Grey-Turner sign, a surgical scar about 6 cm long visible in the lower abdomen, generalized abdominal tenderness and muscle rigidity, no rebound tenderness, liver and spleen not enlarged, no masses palpated, negative for Murphy's sign, negative for succussion splash, negative for shifting dullness, no tenderness in the renal areas, bowel sounds 2 times/min, no borborygmi or high-pitched metallic sounds heard. Genitourinary system and external genitalia not examined. No abnormalities in the spine and limbs, no edema in the lower extremities. Neurological examination did not elicit any pathological signs. Laboratory Tests: Complete blood count: Hb 114 g/L, RBC 3.92 x 10^11/L, WBC 19.7 x 10^9/L, N 0.87, L 0.13, platelets 147 x 10^9/L, bleeding time and clotting time both 1 minute and 30 seconds. Urinalysis: yellow, slightly turbid, specific gravity 1.022, protein (negative), pH 5.0, microscopic examination RBC 0-1/HP, WBC 0-2/HP. Renal function: BUN 9.2 mmol/L, Cr 132 μmol/L. Serum electrolytes: potassium 5.5 mmol/L, sodium 145 mmol/L, chloride 106 mmol/L. Serum amylase: 203.2 units (normal range: 80-180 units), urinary amylase: 1016 units (normal range: 100-1200 units). [Auxiliary Examinations]: Abdominal X-ray: multiple air-fluid levels in the bowel. Abdominal ultrasound: no abnormalities in the liver, gallbladder, pancreas, or spleen. ECG: sinus tachycardia. Diagnostic paracentesis: no fluid aspirated. Please infer the possible initial diagnosis based on the above medical information?

[Chief Complaint]: Gender: Male Age: 38 years
Upper abdominal pain for more than one year, recurrent 4 times [Present Illness]: The patient underwent emergency appendectomy for acute appendicitis on 2010-10-21. At that time, the abdominal pain was severe, and the patient experienced continuous abdominal pain during the surgery and for two days postoperatively. The patient had a low-grade fever of around 37.5-38.5 degrees Celsius postoperatively, and the temperature returned to normal on the fifth day. Antibiotics were used for five days. On 2011-2-11, the patient experienced pain similar to that during the appendicitis, starting with upper abdominal pain, followed by generalized abdominal pain, bloating, no bowel movements, and no flatus. T 38.5 degrees Celsius. No signs of intestinal obstruction were observed on radiography, and bowel motility was normal. Blood examination showed a white blood cell count of 18.8 × 109. The patient was treated with antibiotics for 3-5 days, and the pain subsided. The bloating disappeared. The patient experienced three such recurrent episodes postoperatively, with similar symptoms each time. The most recent episode occurred on 2011-11-28. The night before, the patient drank until 23:00, and the next morning, the patient felt mild abdominal pain after breakfast. The pain in the upper abdomen worsened after dinner that evening, accompanied by bloating. The patient visited the surgical department of our hospital and was diagnosed with gastritis. The patient was treated with intravenous cefoperazone and metronidazole, as in previous episodes. The patient had severe abdominal pain and did not sleep all night on the 28th. On the 29th, the abdominal pain subsided, and the patient started to have a fever of 38.2 degrees Celsius. The patient was given antibiotic treatment again and consulted a surgeon, who still suspected gastritis and prescribed omeprazole. On the 30th, the abdominal pain continued to subside. Due to concern, the patient went to the hospital for a CT scan, which revealed extensive adhesions around the duodenum, encasing the pancreas with severe exudation. The patient was admitted to the hospital that night. Blood amylase levels were normal, and urine amylase was 1109. [Past Medical History]: The patient is a smoker, has a high alcohol intake, and a large appetite. Triglycerides sometimes reach 17.569 mmol/l. Height 177 cm, weight 92 kg. [Physical Examination]: T: 37.5°C, P: 88 beats/min, R: 22 breaths/min, BP: 165/95 mmHg, severe tenderness and rebound tenderness in the right upper abdomen, mild tenderness in the right lower abdomen and left abdomen, and percussion pain in the back. [Auxiliary Examinations]: Biochemical tests showed normal liver and kidney function, lipid levels of 3.69 mmol/l, blood glucose of 6.4, and a blood routine of 14.5 × 109, with 83% neutrophils, and other results were normal. Coagulation profile showed fibrinogen of 9.66 g (normal 2-4 g). Contrast-enhanced CT on the same day showed pancreatitis, with inflammation and enlargement of the pancreatic tail. Ultrasound showed inflammation of the pancreatic tail, measuring 3.6*2.7, with heterogeneous echotexture. Mild to moderate fatty liver. Please infer the possible preliminary diagnosis based on the above medical information?

[Chief Complaint]: Patient ××, male, 45 years old.
Admitted to the hospital due to "a history of liver cirrhosis for 3 years, increased talkativeness, and bilateral lower limb motor dysfunction for more than 3 months." [Present History]: The patient was diagnosed with "post-hepatitis liver cirrhosis" 3 years ago and received traditional Chinese medicine treatment. Three months ago, he developed increased talkativeness, bilateral lower limb edema, a sensation of heaviness as if wrapped, difficulty in lifting feet and walking, presenting with a scissor gait, requiring crutches to stand, and no abnormal sensation in the bilateral lower limbs; poor nighttime sleep. Occasionally, he felt abdominal distension and reduced urine output, with a daily urine volume of 900-1000 ml. One month ago, he visited another hospital, where cerebrospinal fluid examination showed a pressure of 1.37 kPa (143 mmH2O), total cell count of 2×10^6/L, and normal biochemical parameters. Thoracic and lumbar magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and electromyography were both negative. After administration of albumin and diuretics, abdominal distension disappeared, and edema significantly improved, but the motor dysfunction in the bilateral lower limbs did not improve. He had difficulty lifting his legs while lying flat and was unsteady when standing, prone to falls. [Past History]: Twenty years ago, he had hepatitis. Three years ago, esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed esophageal and gastric varices. He has a 25-year history of alcohol consumption, drinking an equivalent of 200 g of pure alcohol daily, but has abstained from alcohol for the past three years. [Physical Examination]: Dull complexion, liver positive, multiple spider nevi scattered on the neck and upper limbs. No obvious abnormalities in the heart and lungs. Abdomen distended, no tenderness, muscle tension, or rebound tenderness, liver enlarged, 2 cm below the costal margin, 7 cm below the xiphoid process, of medium consistency, no obvious tenderness, spleen enlarged, 2 cm below the costal margin, hard in consistency, no splenic friction rub heard, positive shifting dullness. Mild pitting edema in the lower limbs. [Auxiliary Examinations]: Neurological examination: Normal deep and superficial sensation throughout the body, grade V muscle strength in both upper limbs, normal muscle tone, positive flapping tremor in both hands, grade III muscle strength in both lower limbs, increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia of bilateral knee and Achilles tendon reflexes, positive bilateral ankle clonus. Admission auxiliary examinations: WBC 3.1×10^9/L (normal range 4.0—10.0×10^9/L), HB 131 g/L, PLT 43×10^9/L [normal range (100—300)×10^9/L]. Liver function: ALT 62 U/L (normal range 5—40 U/L), AST 109 U/L (normal range 8—40 U/L), TBIL 57.5 µmol/L (normal range 5—20 µmol/L), DBIL 20.4 µmol/L (normal range 1.7—10 µmol/L), ALB 27.7 g/L (normal range 36—55 g/L); PT 16.8 s (normal range 10.7—14.4 s), INR 1.565 (normal range 0.72—1.2). Hepatic virus markers: HBsAg (+), HBsAb (−), blood ammonia 116—120 µmol/L. Enlarged liver, enlarged spleen. Deep venous and inferior vena cava color Doppler ultrasound of both lower limbs. Based on the above clinical information, what is the possible preliminary diagnosis?

[Chief Complaint]: Abdominal pain for 3 days [Present Illness]: The patient developed abdominal pain after drinking alcohol and consuming fatty foods 3 days ago, characterized by continuous dull pain throughout the abdomen, with the umbilical region being the most prominent. Subsequently, the patient experienced abdominal distension, nausea, and a desire to vomit, but no hematemesis or hemoptysis, no chest tightness or palpitations, and no diarrhea. The patient sought medical attention at a local hospital, where an abdominal ultrasound showed no abnormalities, but blood and urine amylase tests revealed elevated urinary amylase levels. At that time, the patient received intravenous therapy (including gastric protection), but the symptoms did not improve. Today, the abdominal pain worsened, and the family brought the patient to our hospital for further treatment. An outpatient examination revealed significantly elevated urinary amylase levels, and the patient was admitted to our department with a presumptive diagnosis of "pancreatitis." Since the onset of the illness, the patient has been conscious, with significant abdominal pain and nausea, no fever or chills, no abnormal sweating or limb convulsions, normal urination, and one episode of suspected black stool. [Past Medical History]: The patient has been generally healthy with no significant medical history, but has a long-term history of smoking and alcohol consumption, smoking 20-40 cigarettes/day, and drinking 200-300 ml/occasion.
Personal History
No significant personal or family history. [Physical Examination]: T: 36.4°C, P: 77 beats/min, R: 21 breaths/min, BP: 150/102 mmHg.
T: 36.4°C, P: 77 beats/min, R: 21 breaths/min, BP: 150/102 mmHg. The patient is alert but appears listless, with a painful expression and appropriate responses to questions. The patient is overweight and was wheeled into the ward, cooperating with the examination. There is no jaundice of the skin or mucous membranes, and no enlarged or tender superficial lymph nodes are palpable; the skull shows no deformity, both pupils are equal and round with a diameter of 3.0 mm and have brisk light reflexes; there is no cyanosis of the lips, and the tongue is midline. The liver and spleen are not palpable below the costal margin, and there is no tenderness at McBurney's point. The shifting dullness is negative, and the bowel sounds are slightly diminished. The spine and limbs show no deformity, with normal movement; the muscle strength in all four limbs is grade 5, muscle tone is normal, physiological reflexes are present, and no pathological reflexes are elicited. There is no edema in the lower extremities. **Rectal and genitalia not examined [Auxiliary Examinations]: Fatty liver; Abdominal plain film: No abnormalities; ECG: Sinus rhythm, T-wave changes; CBC: WBC 15.10x10^9/L, N% 82.31%; AFP and liver function tests are normal, serum amylase is normal, urinary amylase: 757.3 0-500; Cardiac enzyme panel: LDH 109 U/L↓, HBDH 208 U/L↑, troponin I 3 0.23 ng/ml↑↑. [Chief Complaint]: Female, 64 years old, farmer
Intermittent upper abdominal pain for 3 days [Present Illness]: The patient began to experience upper abdominal pain without obvious cause on August 18, 2018. The symptoms were relatively mild, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. The vomitus was gastric contents, non-projectile. There was no dizziness, shortness of breath, cyanosis, jaundice, or referred pain to the shoulder and back. The abdominal pain did not relieve after rest, and she mistakenly thought it was gastritis and self-administered "omeprazole" at home, but saw no improvement. She was urgently admitted to the hospital. The emergency department admitted her with the diagnosis of "to be investigated cause of abdominal pain." During the course of the disease, the patient had a generally poor mental state, poor appetite, no fever, cough, or sputum production, and normal bowel and bladder function. [Past Medical History]: Previously healthy, denies history of "hepatitis" or "tuberculosis." Vaccination history is unknown. Denies history of trauma, surgery, blood transfusion, or administration of blood products. No history of food or drug allergies. [Physical Examination]: T: 36.8°C, P: 64 beats/min, R: 20 breaths/min, BP: 120/60 mmHg. Acutely ill appearance, normal development, moderate nutrition, alert, anxious, answers questions appropriately, cooperative with examination. No obvious jaundice of skin and sclera. Abdominal inspection: flat abdomen, no visible renal or intestinal patterns or peristaltic waves. Palpation: soft abdominal wall, positive tenderness in the gallbladder area, negative Murphy's sign, positive tenderness in the left upper abdomen, more severe than in the gallbladder area. Liver and spleen not palpable below the costal margin, no masses palpable. Percussion: no shifting dullness, no tenderness on percussion in the liver, spleen, and bilateral renal areas. Auscultation: bowel sounds 3 times/min, no vascular murmur heard in the abdomen. [Auxiliary Examinations]: Abdominal ultrasound (August 21, 2018, this hospital) enlarged pancreatic volume (inflammation?), mild dilation of intrahepatic bile ducts, full gallbladder, main pancreatic duct dilation, fatty liver, right pleural effusion. Urinary amylase: amylase 22190.88 U/L, serum amylase: amylase 3473.80 U/L. Please infer the patient's possible preliminary diagnosis based on the above medical information?

[Chief Complaint]: Middle-aged male patient, acute onset.
Admitted due to "left upper quadrant pain for one day." [Current Medical History]: The patient began experiencing left upper quadrant pain at 9 AM on February 5, 2014, which was continuous and progressively worsened, accompanied by abdominal distension, nausea, and vomiting. The vomitus was non-coffee-ground gastric contents, without heartburn, belching, or acid regurgitation, and without palpitations, chest tightness, chills, or fever. The patient sought medical attention at a hospital, [Past Medical History]: None. [Physical Examination]: Alert, poor mental status, acute appearance, upper abdominal distension. The patient began to have recurrent fever on February 19, 2014, with a peak temperature of 39.7°C. Initially treated with imipenem, then switched to meropenem, and finally treated with imipenem and levofloxacin, but the patient continued to have recurrent fever. Blood culture did not yield any bacteria. Ascites examination was between transudate and exudate. Ascites culture results are pending. Blood was drawn today for fungal antigen testing. [Auxiliary Examinations]: None. Please infer the possible preliminary diagnosis based on the above medical information?

[Chief Complaint]: Male, 30 years old.
Presented with abdominal pain for 6 hours, worsened 1 hour ago. [History of Present Illness]: The patient suddenly experienced abdominal pain 6 hours ago, predominantly in the left upper quadrant, accompanied by vomiting of gastric contents, without diarrhea. He was treated at a local clinic, and his symptoms improved. One hour ago, the symptoms reappeared with acute exacerbation. The local clinic suspected urinary calculi. [Past Medical History]: None. [Physical Examination]: Vital signs stable, tenderness in the upper left abdomen, no significant rebound tenderness or muscle tension. Bowel sounds present. [Chief Complaint]: Mr. Wang, male, 74 years old, was admitted to the emergency department due to "recurrent abdominal pain for 2 months, worsened with cessation of flatus and defecation for 4 days".

[Present History]: Two months before admission, the patient developed abdominal pain without any obvious cause. The pain was dull, mainly located in the upper middle abdomen and around the umbilicus, and was tolerable. It was accompanied by abdominal distension, but there was no chills, fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or melena. He received "fluid replacement and anti-inflammatory" treatment at a local hospital, and his symptoms improved. Four days ago, the patient experienced abdominal pain again, which was more severe than before. There was still no nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or melena, but he developed cessation of flatus and defecation. He received treatment at a local hospital (details unknown), but his symptoms did not improve, so he came to our hospital. Since the onset of the illness, the patient's mental state, appetite, and sleep have been acceptable, but he has lost 15 kg in weight.

[Medical History]: More than 5 years ago, the patient was found to have "heart disease" (details unknown) and has been on long-term treatment with "Cardiokang" and "Danshen tablets." He has also been on long-term medication for "benign prostatic hyperplasia."

[Physical Examination]: T: 36.5°C, P: 84 beats/min, R: 20 breaths/min, BP: 141/86 mmHg. The patient was alert, with no abnormalities in the heart and lungs. The abdomen was soft, with mild tenderness throughout, most prominent in the upper middle abdomen. Bowel pattern was visible, with no peristaltic waves. There was distension in the lower abdomen, and shifting dullness was positive. Bowel sounds were hyperactive, and high-pitched bowel sounds were occasionally heard. Neurological examination was negative.

[Supportive Examinations]: Emergency abdominal plain film: Partial bowel dilation in the abdominal cavity, with visible air-fluid levels. The psoas muscle lines and peritoneal fat lines were clear, but the pelvic fat line was indistinct. No free gas was seen in the abdominal cavity. RBC 3.66x1012/L; Hb 120g/L; PLT 73g/L; WBC 10.7x109/L; Na 131.9mmol/L; coagulation function was normal.

Please infer the possible initial diagnosis based on the above clinical information.

[Chief Complaint]: Female patient, 30 years old
Admitted to our hospital on December 19, 2012, with "slightly rounded face, weight gain for 4 years, and fractures for 2 years." [Present Illness]: The patient gradually developed weight gain in 2008, accompanied by a slightly rounded face, increased waist circumference, and easy bruising after minor collisions. In August 2010, she fell down the stairs and sustained a fracture of the base of the right little finger. In March 2012, she slipped and sustained a fracture of the right humeral lateral epicondylar neck. On May 3, 2012, she visited our hospital due to recurrent fractures and was diagnosed with "osteopenia, history of fractures, and vitamin D deficiency." She was prescribed calcium carbonate D3 (Caltrate D) 0.6g once daily, cholecalciferol emulsion (Inkangli) 1ml every two weeks, and alendronate sodium (Fosamax) 7mg once weekly. On September 3, 2012, she had blood calcium 2.41mmol/L, blood phosphorus 0.84mmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 74U/L, parathyroid hormone 146ng/L, 24-hour urine free cortisol 282.8nmol (normal range 28-276nmol), and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) 9.9pmol/L. Due to elevated parathyroid hormone, she was prescribed calcium carbonate D3 0.6g twice daily and calcitriol 0.25μg twice daily. After 7 days, the parathyroid hormone remained at 131ng/L. On October 29, 2012, plasma ACTH was 14.7pmol/L, and plasma cortisol was 770.6nmol/L. She was admitted to the hospital for further investigation of "elevated parathyroid hormone of unknown cause?
